<p class="eyebrow">Plotting / fluxplot</p>

# Lines, points and distributions

::: {.doc-lead}
Choose a plotting helper, name the series, and keep its parts editable.
:::

Every helper is a thin wrapper over a Matplotlib call that takes a `series=` name, so the saved plot knows which line, point or bar is which. A complete plot (the values are synthetic):

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import fluxplot as fp

fp.use_paper()
x = np.linspace(0, 10, 50)
mean = np.exp(-x / 4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(3.2, 2.4), layout="constrained")
fp.line(ax, x, mean, series="control", label="Control")
fp.band(ax, x, mean * 0.9, mean * 1.1, series="control", what="95% CI")
fp.scatter(ax, x[::5], mean[::5] + 0.03, series="observed", label="Observed")
ax.set(xlabel="Time (s)", ylabel="Response")
fp.legend(ax)
fp.save(fig, "plots/response.svg")
```

## Choose a helper {#choose-a-helper}

The helpers return ordinary Matplotlib artists. Every series gets a stable name. Use `label=` for the text you want in a legend.

| What you need | Function |
|---|---|
| Connected observations | `fp.line`, `fp.step`, `fp.stem` |
| Individual points | `fp.scatter` |
| Vertical or horizontal bars | `fp.bar`, `fp.barh` |
| Uncertainty | `fp.errorbar`, `fp.band` |
| A filled region | `fp.area` |
| A distribution | `fp.hist`, `fp.box`, `fp.violin`, `fp.kde` |
| A fitted relationship | `fp.regression` |
| Reference marks and labels | `fp.reference_line`, `fp.annotation`, `fp.legend` |

See the [API reference](/docs/fluxplot-api.html) for each signature. The examples below assume `import matplotlib.pyplot as plt` and `import fluxplot as fp`, an axes `ax`, and data variables from your own analysis.

## Lines and uncertainty {#lines-and-uncertainty}

```python
fp.line(ax, x, mean, series="control", label="Control")
fp.band(ax, x, lower, upper, series="control", what="95% CI")
fp.legend(ax)
```

The band and line share a series identity. The band records its bounds and what they mean (`what=`); it does not calculate a confidence interval for you. `fp.errorbar` records scalar, symmetric or asymmetric errors and separately names its line, points, caps and bars. `fp.area` records the two boundaries of a filled region.

## Points and categories {#points-and-categories}

`fp.scatter` gives individual points identities. Supply stable point IDs when row order may change; see [semantic IDs](/docs/plot-format.html#semantic-ids-the-universal-join-key). Categorical and date axes retain display labels alongside numeric coordinates. Bar plots record centres, widths, baselines, lengths and category keys.

On a log axis, use a positive baseline: a bar that starts at zero has no valid position on a log scale. For counts of at least one, draw the bars from 1 with `ax.barh(y, counts - 1, left=1)`, then name each bar with `fp.tag`.

## Distributions and fits {#distributions-and-fits}

`fp.hist` records its actual bin edges and heights, including density, weights and cumulative settings. `fp.box` and `fp.violin` name their components. These helpers include raw sample values only when you choose `include_values=True`.

`fp.regression` supports linear, polynomial and LOWESS fits. Its optional band is a confidence interval for the mean response, using a seeded bootstrap for LOWESS. The manifest records the fit, coefficients, grid, sample size and interval. `fp.kde` records a Gaussian kernel-density estimate and its bandwidth.

For individual observations alongside a mean with its uncertainty or a box plot, use the [meanmark or fluxbox](/docs/signature-plots.html). For inferential comparisons, see [statistics](/docs/statistics.html).

## Axes, insets and legends {#axes-insets-and-legends}

Name multi-panel axes with `fp.panel(ax, name="response")`. Insets retain their host panel. `fp.secondary_axis` records the sampled parent-to-secondary transform. A normal `twinx()` or `twiny()` remains part of its parent panel, with a second value axis; explicitly naming the twin makes it a separate panel.

Figure titles, shared axis labels, figure legends and figure annotations receive figure-level identities. `fp.legend` keeps a legend entry connected to the artist it represents, including hand-picked handles.

## Existing Matplotlib artists {#existing-matplotlib-artists}

```python
line, = ax.plot(x, prediction, "--", color="black")
fp.tag(line, role="reference-line", name="model")
points = ax.scatter(x, observations)
fp.tag_points(points, series="observations")
```

A public, unique Matplotlib label can also become a series at save time. Unlabeled or ambiguously labeled artists remain generic parts. fluxplot does not infer scientific meaning from colour or geometry: name an uncertainty band, fit or threshold explicitly.

## Seaborn {#seaborn}

```python
import seaborn as sns

# df is a pandas DataFrame from your analysis.
sns.lineplot(data=df, x="time", y="signal", hue="region", ax=ax)
fp.tag_seaborn(ax, plot="lineplot")
```

Supported adapters include line, scatter, bar, histogram, KDE and regression plots, plus box, violin, strip, swarm and point plots. For categorical plots, pass the original frame and column names so identity follows the data:

```python
sns.swarmplot(data=df, x="group", y="value", hue="sex", ax=ax)
fp.tag_seaborn(ax, plot="swarmplot", data=df,
               x="group", y="value", hue="sex")
```

With a hue, each hue level becomes a series and categories become named parts. Without a hue, each category becomes a series. Mixed scatter collections can retain the original artist while assigning the appropriate point identities to each group.

## Other plot types {#other-plot-types}

`fp.tag` covers any Matplotlib artist. Tag stackplot layers as areas, hexbin collections as a field, or each ridge's fill and outline under one series. Custom roles can use an `x-` prefix. For live matrix cells and colour controls, prefer the dedicated [field helpers](/docs/matrices-and-scales.html).
